headline: Ippan is Middle Chinese 一般, literally “one + sort”.
Sakan is a sound shift from 盛り (sakari), sharing a root with 栄える (sakaeru, “to thrive”) and 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).
Saraishū is analyzed as either 再来 (sarai, “two next”) plus 週, or 再 (sa, “again”) plus 来週 (raishū); first attested in 1966.
Sentā is borrowed from English center, centre.
Musume is analyzed as 生す (musu, “to beget”) plus 女 (me, “female”).
Genshō is from Middle Chinese 現象 (MC henH zjangX).
Shoho is from Middle Chinese 初步.
Masumasu is a reduplication of 増す (masu).
Shikashi is possibly a shift from 然り (shikari, “being like so”) plus し.
Kōkōsei is 高校 (kōkō, “high school”) plus 生 (-sei, “student; pupil”).
Umare is the continuative stem of 生まれる (umareru, “to be born”).
Suijōki is 水 (sui, “water”) plus 蒸気 (jōki, “steam, vapor”).
Imēji is borrowed from English image, possibly with -age mispronounced as in page and stage.
Oru was woru in Old Japanese, written with the phonetic man'yōgana 袁理 in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Sara is attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the phonetic spelling 娑羅.
Kakudai is 拡 (kaku, “expand”) plus 大 (dai, “big”).
Toire is a clipping of トイレット (toiretto), borrowed from English toilet.
Naru, “to become”, is related to 生る (naru).
Hone went from pone through ɸone to hone, from Proto-Japonic *pənay.
Enchō is 延 (en, “to extend”) plus 長 (chō, “long”).
Tsukamaru is related to 掴まる (tsukamaru), both originally from 束 (tsuka, “bundle”).
Yatto may begin with a shortening of 漸く (yōyaku, “at last, finally, barely”).
Otoko no hito is 男 (otoko, “male person, man”) plus の (no) plus 人 (hito, “person”).
Kansai is literally “west of 逢坂の関 (Ōsaka-no-seki, “tollgate of Ōsaka-yama”)”.
Odokasu is compared with 驚く (odoroku, “to surprise”).
Tanoshimi is the stem form of the verb 楽しむ (“to enjoy”).
Dōro went from dauro to dɔːro to doːro, from Middle Chinese 道路.
Moshimo is もし (moshi, “if”) plus も (mo, “also, too, even”).
Iwa went from ipa to ifa to iwa, from Old Japanese.
Genjitsu is from the Middle Chinese compound 現實.
